items.scenario: You open Notation Hero in Berlin and press 'No, send nothing'. A week later you open it again on the same laptop, which now shows New York time after a trip. No question appears, Google Analytics counts your visit, and Sentry may report your errors. Your 'No' is still saved in the browser, but the rule reads it only when the clock says Europe.
items.whats_wrong: Section 2's table gives 'Outside Europe' everything and has no row for a saved answer. allowed() is defined as that table, and its unit test checks exactly its 15 cells. So a saved 'Report errors only' or 'No, send nothing' is ignored whenever the browser's time zone is outside Europe: after a trip, after a time-zone change, and later for every 'No' that NH-349's link saves for a visitor outside Europe, which its Jira ticket promises.

GDPR Article 7(3): 'Prior to giving consent, the data subject shall be informed thereof' (https://gdpr-info.eu/art-7-gdpr/). The CNIL (https://www.cnil.fr/fr/cookies-et-autres-traceurs/regles/cookies/que-dit-la-loi) lists 'l'identité des responsables du ou des traitements' and the means to 'retirer son consentement'. items.correction: The effect holds; the reason given is out of date. WebKit's 2019 rule capped cookies written by a script at a 7-day expiry (Intelligent Tracking Prevention, ITP 2.1). A 2022 WebKit release removed that cap and now deletes cookies written by a script, together with all other storage a script can write (localStorage too), when the site gets no click, tap or key press during 7 days of browser use. So a visitor who returns after a week without using the site still counts as new, and the same rule also deletes the saved privacy answer, so a visitor in Europe is asked again.

items.central_claim_check: WebKit's tracking-prevention page today, section '7-Day Cap on All Script-Writeable Storage': 'ITP deletes all cookies created in JavaScript and all other script-writeable storage after 7 days of no user interaction with the website' (https://webkit.org/tracking-prevention/). The 2019 expiry cap: 'all persistent client-side cookies, i.e. persistent cookies created through document.cookie, are capped to a seven day expiry' (https://webkit.org/blog/8613/intelligent-tracking-prevention-2-1/). The 2020 rule for other storage, LocalStorage included: deleted 'after seven days of Safari use without user interaction on the site' (https://webkit.org/blog/10218/full-third-party-cookie-blocking-and-more/). The 2022 change from the cap to deletion: https://www.simoahava.com/privacy/first-party-cookies-webkit-revisited/ (14 November 2022; a secondary source quoting WebKit's documentation). Other iPhone and iPad browsers: since iOS 14 they get the same rules through WebKit's WKWebView (https://www.simoahava.com/privacy/intelligent-tracking-prevention-ios-14-ipados-14-safari-14/, secondary). `_ga` is written by script: in the R1 spike it appeared although every collect request was answered locally with no Set-Cookie header. Safari's deletion itself is (untested) here.
items.contradicts: none — checked goal 1 (38), section 2's 'Kept in this browser' (130-132), section 7's 'a lasting ID' (330; still true outside WebKit browsers) and Known limits (420-431).

spike.what: The R1 spike (Chromium, Google's real gtag.js, a made-up ID, every collect request answered locally) recorded the cookies after the first page view.
spike.result: `_ga` and `_ga_<ID>` were set although no response carried a Set-Cookie header, so gtag.js writes them by script — the kind WebKit deletes. Safari's 7-day deletion itself was not run: Playwright's WebKit build is not Safari, so it is (untested) and rests on WebKit's documentation.

On Safari, and on iPhones and iPads, it is not: WebKit deletes cookies written by a script, such as `_ga`, and the site's localStorage after 7 days of browser use without the visitor using the site. Returning visitors are undercounted, the saved answer disappears, and the spec says neither.

items.central_claim_check: True. quotes.quote: a consent update to denied
Google's "advanced" consent mode (a small site never reaches its modelling thresholds, and EU guidance says those pings need consent too)

items.central_claim_check: True. Google's 'Consent mode on websites and mobile apps' (https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9976101): with analytics_storage denied the tag 'Will not read or write first-party analytics cookies' and 'cookieless pings will be sent to Google Analytics'. Google's consent-mode concepts page (https://developers.google.com/tag-platform/security/concepts/consent-mode): 'While consent is denied, the Google tags send measurements without cookies.' Neither page describes an update from granted to denied after the tag has loaded; the spike did, and the tag kept sending. Google's switch to stop the tag (https://developers.google.com/tag-platform/security/guides/privacy, updated 2026-07-30): window['ga-disable-MEASUREMENT_ID'] = true 'turns off the Google tag from sending data', and it 'must be set before any calls to gtag() are made'.
items.contradicts: none — checked G3 (58: the fix keeps out the cookieless pings G3 rejected), section 4 (track() sends nothing once stopped) and Known limits. NH-349 itself is out of scope here.

spike.what: A scratch Node script drove Playwright 1.61.1's Chromium from web/node_modules. It loaded Google's real gtag.js for a made-up ID, fetched through Playwright's route.fetch() (the only network traffic: GET requests for the script), with the spec's consent default and settings. Every collect request was answered locally (204) and recorded; Chromium's resolver mapped every other host to NOTFOUND, and no other request was seen. Runs: (A) consent update to denied, then one gtag('event'); (B) consent update to denied, no more calls from our code, then the page is left; (C) consent update to denied plus window['ga-disable-G-…'] = true, set after the tag had loaded, then one gtag('event') and the page is left.
spike.result: (A) Before the update: page_view and an event, gcs=G101, the cookie's client ID. After it: the event was still sent, gcs=G100, with a new temporary client ID; leaving the page sent user_engagement (gcs=G100) to www.google-analytics.com/g/collect and www.google.com/g/collect. (B) With no call from our code, leaving the page still sent user_engagement (gcs=G100) to both hosts. (C) After ga-disable: no request at all — neither the event nor the hit on leaving. In every run the `_ga` and `_ga_<ID>` cookies stayed.

items.scenario: Later, a 'Privacy choices' link (NH-349) lets you change 'Yes' to 'No' while the player is open. This spec tells that ticket to send Google a 'consent: denied' update and stop sending events. You press 'No' and keep practising. When you close the tab, Google Analytics still sends one more report about your visit, only without its cookie — the kind of report this spec's G3 decided also needs consent.
items.whats_wrong: 'Extending later' tells NH-349 that changing to 'No' stops Google Analytics with 'a consent update to denied, and no more events'. A Google tag that is already loaded keeps sending cookieless pings after that update: in the spike, a user_engagement hit each time the page is left, with no call from our code. G3 rejected those pings because EU guidance says they need consent too.

before.text:
- **NH-349's link** reuses `PrivacyChoices` and `saveChoice()`. Changing to "No" must stop Google
  Analytics (a consent update to denied, and no more events) and close Sentry for the rest of the
  visit.

after.text:
- **NH-349's link** reuses `PrivacyChoices` and `saveChoice()`. Changing to "No" must stop Google
  Analytics for the rest of the visit. A consent update to denied is not enough: the loaded tag
  still sends a cookieless `user_engagement` hit when the page is left (spike, 2026-10-08). So the
  link also sets `window['ga-disable-<ID>'] = true` and sends no more events. Google documents that
  switch as set before any `gtag()` call, so NH-349's test must prove no hit follows a "No". The
  link must also close Sentry for the rest of the visit.

items.proposed_fix: Tell NH-349 to stop the tag, not only update consent: send the update, set window['ga-disable-<ID>'] = true, send no more events, and prove in a test that no hit follows a 'No'.
items.why_it_works: In the spike, setting the switch after the tag had loaded stopped every later hit, including the automatic one sent when the page is left. A test is still needed, because Google documents the switch as set before any gtag() call. On later page loads, allowed() keeps Google Analytics from starting at all.

plain_terms.gcs: the consent code in each Google Analytics request: G101 = ad storage denied, analytics granted; G100 = both denied
plain_terms.user_engagement: an event the Google tag sends by itself when a page is left, with the time spent on it
plain_terms.ga-disable-<ID>: Google's documented switch, window['ga-disable-<measurement ID>'] = true, that stops the tag sending data
plain_terms.G3: decision G3: Europe is asked first; it rejected Google's 'advanced' consent mode because its cookieless pings need consent too
plain_terms.NH-349: the Jira ticket for a "Privacy choices" link that lets any visitor, in or outside Europe, change their answer later; status To Do (Jira, read 2026-10-08)

severity_check.why: Guidance for a later ticket; cheap to correct now, and as written it would mislead NH-349's implementer.

cross_fix: F-1 — F-1 makes a 'No' hold on the next page loads; this fix stops the tag on the page where the answer changes. NH-349 needs both.
The `_ga` cookies stay after a 'No' (spike). They are not read again once Google Analytics no longer starts; deleting them is a choice for NH-349's plan, not part of this fix.
